A cask called Father Christmas

A Wrexham landlady christened a cask Father Christmas and tapped it on Christmas Eve. Christmas ale was never a style. It was a date, a strength and a piece of theatre.

On Christmas Eve 1858, in Wrexham, a cask of beer was given a name.

Mrs Rowland of the Nag’s Head had been advertising for about a week. Her Christmas ale would please the palate and please the eye by its sparkling brilliancy, and would warm and invigorate the whole system. And then the detail that makes it a story rather than a notice: the large cask containing two hundred gallons, and christened Father Christmas, would be tapped on Christmas Eve.

The advert ran under a verse.

Hail! Father Christmas, Hail! to thee, / Honoured ever shalt thou be; / All the sweets that love bestows, / Endless pleasures wait on those / Who, like the vassals brave and true, / Give to Christmas homage due.Wrexham and Denbighshire Advertiser, 24 December 1858

The following Christmas Eve, the Nag’s Head was illuminated from six till eleven for the tapping, and the lovers of the pure extract of malt and hops were respectfully invited to come and taste it. The cask had grown, though by how much depends on the scan: five hundred gallons on our reading of it, six hundred on the archive’s transcription.

Not a style, a date

It is tempting to read all this as evidence of a Victorian beer style. Gary Gillman puts the case against it plainly: Christmas ale was never, in other words, a fixed style or type, and at best it might mean something special made available at Christmas.

The strongest thing in the record is an absence. We searched twelve British brewing manuals of the period for the words Christmas, Xmas and Yule: Black, Wigney, Chadwick, Hitchcock, Tizard, Pitt, Southby, Accum, Child, Roberts, Byrn and The Brewer of 1874. We have not found Christmas ale in any of them. The only hits are men keeping Christmas somewhere, which is not a beer.

Everything the Wrexham adverts boast about is in those manuals under other names. Strength is there as stock ale and strong ale. Long ageing is there. October brewing is there, because October was when you brewed what you meant to keep. What is not there is a product called Christmas ale, because Christmas ale was not a thing you brewed. It was a thing you sold.

The habit is older than those manuals. One of 1700, Directions for Brewing Malt Liquors, quoted by Ron Pattinson in The Home Brewer’s Guide to Vintage Beer, has its author broaching by the calendar rather than by the recipe. He keeps his beer about nine months, and so takes “my March Beer at Christmas, and my October Beer at Midsummer, at which times it is generally at the best”. Christmas is not something he brews. It is when he opens the cask.

Which is exactly what the adverts are doing. They sell the tapping, not the recipe. Tapped this day. Tapped on Christmas Eve. Orders should be given immediately. The Wrexham Brewery Company, in 1880, promised delivery a fortnight before Christmas Day. In 1869 the Nag’s Head finally says the quiet part out loud and advertises beer brewed in October and matured on the stillage, which is the whole of the method, stated as a selling point rather than a style.

What it cost, and how strong

The price evidence is thin and consistent, which is the best combination available.

The late Martyn Cornell’s reading of Victorian beer adverts puts Christmas ale in the top price tier, alongside No 1 Burton and imperial stout, at two shillings a gallon and an original gravity above 1100. He is careful that not every brewer sold every beer at every price point, and the Wrexham adverts never quote a gravity or a price at all, so the Nag’s Head ale cannot be put on that scale.

Where a number does survive, it is large. Ron Pattinson owns a brewing log from Lovibond, a small London brewer, containing an XXXX ale whose record states it was for Christmas. It was brewed on 7 October 1864, at an original gravity of 1096. Cornell found a Watford brewer selling an XXXXX Christmas Ale at two shillings a gallon in the 1890s, and reasoned from the price that it must have been over 1100.

And on 23 December 1853 Parker and Twining of Pall Mall advertised in The Standard, under the heading Allsopp’s Ales for Christmas, a small stock of “the STRONG CHRISTMAS ALE” to be sent out as a curiosity for Christmas consumption, originally brewed for the Czar Peter and the Empress Catherine, many barrels of which had gone by order of the Admiralty with the expedition sent in search of Sir John Franklin. The advert gives the beer no other name. Martyn Cornell, who found it, identifies it as Allsopp’s Arctic Ale and gives its price as forty-five shillings per eighteen-gallon kilderkin, two and a half times more than the cost of ordinary porter. It is the beer we have written about, revived in the last few years on a provenance nobody can quite produce.

The phrase is older than the product

William Sandys, writing on Christmastide, has it that Christmas broached the mightiest ale and that Christmas ale “has, accordingly, been famous from the earliest times”. Welsh papers use the phrase in verse and folklore in 1838, 1839 and 1852, before any of the adverts here.

So the Victorian brewers were not naming something new. They were taking a phrase every reader already knew from carols and country custom, and putting it on a cask.

A warning for anyone counting: Welsh newspaper OCR reads CHRISTMAS SALE as CHRISTMAS ALE, and the Wrexham cattle market ran a Christmas sale of fat stock in 1877. Any keyword count of the phrase is contaminated by livestock.

The row about the workhouse

The best of it is not in the adverts at all.

On 19 December 1861 the Wrexham Board of Guardians read out letters offering Christmas beer for the workhouse. A publican at the Golden Lion Vaults offered a kilderkin of the best XX stout. A brewer at Wrexham Fechan offered a half barrel of the best beer. So did the Carnarvon Castle Inn. And so did Thomas Rowland of the Nag’s Head, who had worked out why the offers had dried up.

He had heard, he wrote, that no Wrexham brewer intended to send the usual half barrel for the poor on Christmas Day, because of the opposition to be expected from his very enthusiastic teetotal friend, Mr Lester, who would substitute plum cake and coffee instead of beer. Rowland noted that Scripture says wine maketh glad the heart of man, observed that he had no wine, and offered a half barrel of ale, out of his turn, to make glad if possible the hearts of the poor people.

There were a hundred and seventy people in the house.

That argument did not go away. At Cardiff’s workhouse in 1909, the men got a pint of ale with Christmas dinner and the women half a pint. In Colchester in 1922, a pint a head was carried by twelve votes to five. For sixty years, whether the poor got a Christmas drink was decided by a show of hands.

The scale is easy to miss. Martyn Cornell found that on Christmas Day 1860, between forty and fifty thousand inmates of the metropolitan workhouses were served roast beef and plum pudding, and that the meal of beef, pudding and ale had become an institution by the middle of the century.

Where it went

The phrase does not fade in the nineteenth century. In 1898 a South Wales columnist is still saying that the good old custom of drinking Christmas ale has not faded in any way by the march of the years, and then grumbling about beer and recommending light wines, which is its own kind of evidence.

What changes is the container. The Brewery History Society puts the earliest known festive bottled beer in the 1930s, either a Christmas Ale from John Fox of Ewloe or one from Simonds, and cannot say which came first because neither is dated. Before that, as the Society puts it, generic strong ales not specifically associated with Christmas had been an integral part of winter for years.

The beer came first and the label came later.

Will Hawkes gives Harvey’s Christmas Ale, first brewed in 1972 by their head brewer Anthony Jenner, as one of the oldest British Christmas ales still in production, if not the oldest. The wider revival waits for the small breweries. Cornell, quoted by Matthew Curtis, dates it: it was not until the small brewery revival began to take off in the 1980s that drinkers in Britain were again offered a range of Christmas special beers. And the nearest thing to it on a bar now is not called Christmas anything: it is Young’s Winter Warmer, which Cornell in 2007 counted among the few surviving brother beers in the Burton ale style, alongside Marston’s Owd Roger and Theakston’s Old Peculier. It is now brewed by Carlsberg Britvic at the Albion Brewery in Burton on Trent, on a site dating from 1834. Carlsberg Britvic has proposed closing the Burton brewery in summer 2027, with the possible loss of up to three hundred jobs. The cask brands may be contracted out.

Twelve beers, nine styles

Beers of Europe sells a mixed case called 12 Beers of Christmas UK. In November 2026 it held a smoked porter, an English porter, a second English porter, a porter the catalogue files under other, a pastry stout, a Scottish ale, a dark lager, an English pale ale, a winter warmer and three winter ales. Nine styles between twelve bottles.

They do not share a strength either. The case runs from 4.1 per cent to 6 per cent, which at the bottom end is ordinary bitter. The Victorian Christmas ale was known by its gravity. This one is known by its label: Sledgehammer, Bad Elf, Merry X-Moose, Santas Porter, White Christmas.

In Wrexham the brewery behind the Nag’s Head went in 1984, when Marston’s took over Border Breweries and closed the site. The pub is still there on Mount Street, and Marston’s still run it, and it still does a Christmas menu.

Read the sign

In Wrexham, a landlady named a cask Father Christmas. The following year, the Nag’s Head was lit up for the Christmas tapping. In London, a bust of Dickens stands on a pub built on the spot where he once bought a glass of ale. In Hogarth’s Beer Street, part of a brewer’s name is still legible. And in Stockport, Robinsons put a name already used for gin on a strong ale. And in Sonoma, a brewer who said a brewery without a history could invent one chose a name that already had two.

Five stories about what a name can tell you, and what it can’t.
